ConocoPhillips fell 1% today to close at $131.83, extending a sharp two-week decline of nearly 3%. The immediate driver is an easing in Middle East supply fears: after Saudi Arabia was hit with attacks on its pipeline infrastructure this week, the kingdom signaled it would boost crude exports through the Strait of Hormuz to compensate, which calmed market anxiety about a major supply disruption. Oil prices reflected this relief—US crude sits at $107 per barrel, down from earlier highs—and the stock has retreated accordingly over the past few days as geopolitical risk premiums came out of the market.

The broader context is that while Middle East tensions remain real (fresh Saudi-Houthi clashes and now reports of incidents near Riyadh airport), the market is now pricing in Saudi production staying online rather than being knocked offline. For an oil major like ConocoPhillips, lower oil prices and reduced volatility typically mean lower near-term earnings potential, even though stable supplies are generally better for long-term business than crisis scenarios.
